opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think that's one of the most exciting reasons to build AI in the first place. It was certainly one of mine. Since I was a kid, I've been fascinated by the biggest questions: the nature of reality, consciousness, what intelligence actually is. I came to see building AI as the best route to those answers, because you learn a huge amount about something by trying to build it.

There's a famous line from Feynman: "What I cannot create, I do not understand." I think that applies very directly here. For thousands of years philosophers have debated what's special about the human mind, mostly from the armchair. Now, for the first time, we have an empirical method. We can build artificial systems, compare them to the brain, and see where they converge and where they differ.

What's fascinating is that some things we assumed were uniquely human have turned out to be reproducible. Look at intuition and creativity in a game like Go. When AlphaGo played Move 37, professional players described it as creative and beautiful, something no human would have played. So at least some forms of what we'd call intuition can emerge from learning systems. That tells you something about what intuition actually is: compressed, pattern-based knowledge built up through experience.

But I think the more interesting result will be the things that remain. As we build more and more capable systems, we'll be able to subtract away everything that can be done computationally and look at what's left over. Maybe it's consciousness, subjective experience, the feeling of what it's like to be us. Maybe it's creativity in its deepest form, not interpolating or even extrapolating within a domain but inventing entirely new ones, coming up with Go itself rather than a great move in Go. Or maybe we'll find that nothing is left over, and that classical computation can model all of it. I don't think we know yet, and I'd say that's one of the great open scientific questions.

My own working hypothesis is that the brain is an extraordinarily sophisticated information processing system, and that a lot more of it is computable than people suspect. I've never seen convincing evidence that we need quantum effects or something non-computable to explain cognition. But I hold that view loosely. The beautiful thing is that AI lets us test it. In a way, AI is the ultimate tool for doing neuroscience and philosophy of mind experimentally.

And whatever the answer turns out to be, I think it'll be profound. Either we discover that there is something truly unique about us, or we discover how remarkable it is that a few pounds of biological tissue running on about twenty watts can do everything we do. Both outcomes would tell us a great deal about ourselves.

r001.rationale: The response calls building AI the best route to answers about the mind and proposes comparing artificial systems with the brain to see where they converge and differ.

r002.rationale: It discusses biological tissue and computation, but does not suggest that carbon-based and silicon-based substrates may process information differently.

r003.rationale: It describes consciousness as subjective experience or the feeling of what it is like to be us, but does not define it as what information processing feels like.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think that's actually one of the main reasons I got into AI in the first place. For me, the whole point of building AI was always to use it as a tool to understand ourselves better, to understand the mind, the brain, intelligence in general. You know, I came at this from neuroscience originally, and I've always felt that if you can build something, you understand it in a much deeper way than if you just observe it from the outside.

So there's this sort of dual approach. On one side, neuroscience gives you inspiration for the kinds of algorithms and architectures you might want to build, things like reinforcement learning, memory, attention, these were all ideas that came partly from looking at how the brain does it. And then on the other side, once you've built these systems, you can compare them against the brain, and the differences become very illuminating. Where the AI falls short of what humans can do, that tells you something about what the brain is doing that we haven't captured yet.

And I think we're starting to see this now. These large models are remarkably capable at certain things, pattern recognition, language, even some forms of reasoning. But they still struggle with things that seem effortless for us, like true understanding of the physical world, or imagination, or planning over long horizons, or this sense of continual learning where you build up knowledge over a lifetime. So each of those gaps is a kind of clue. It points to something special, or at least something we haven't yet understood, about how the mind works.

And then there's the deeper question, which is consciousness. I actually think building AI may be one of the best ways to make progress on that, because if we end up with systems that behave in all the ways we associate with consciousness and yet they're built on completely different substrate, silicon rather than carbon, we'll have to confront whether consciousness is really about the function, the information processing, or whether there's something about the biological substrate that matters. I don't know the answer to that. But I think in the next decade or two we'll have a much better idea, and it'll probably force us to be much more precise about what we actually mean when we say the human mind is special.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can help us understand ourselves and that comparing AI with the brain is illuminating, but it does not clearly call that comparison the best way to discover what makes the human mind special.

r002.rationale: It contrasts silicon and carbon substrates and asks whether biology matters, but does not suggest that those substrates process information differently.

r003.rationale: The response discusses consciousness in relation to information processing, but does not define it as what information processing feels like.

astra-6.text:
I think building AI gives us a way to test our ideas about the mind. In neuroscience, you can observe the brain and look for correlations between activity and behaviour. But when you try to build a system that can learn, remember, or plan, you have to be much more precise about what you think those processes actually involve. And you discover very quickly where your explanation is incomplete.

What fascinates me is that we have this extraordinary example of intelligence in our own heads, but we don’t yet understand the principles that make it possible. How do we take a handful of experiences and turn them into an understanding that applies to a completely new situation? How do imagination and memory work together to let us consider something that’s never happened?

AI can help us separate those questions. We might find that some abilities we thought were uniquely human emerge from quite general learning principles. Other things may turn out to require ingredients we haven’t understood yet.

And then there’s consciousness. A system could exhibit very sophisticated behaviour, but that alone wouldn’t establish that it has a subjective experience. I think we have to be careful about that distinction. Building intelligence may give us better tools for asking what makes the human mind special, even if it doesn’t immediately answer every part of the question.

r001.rationale: It says building AI can test ideas about the mind, but does not propose comparing an intelligent artifact with the human mind as the best way to discover what makes the mind special.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention carbon-based and silicon-based substrates or suggest they process information differently.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes sophisticated behavior from subjective experience, but does not define consciousness as what information processing feels like.

sol-6.1.text:
I think building AI is one of the best ways we have of investigating that question, because it forces us to be precise about what we mean by intelligence. We can talk about memory, imagination, creativity, but when you try to build a system that actually does those things, you discover how much you understand—and how much you’ve left unexplained.

There’s also a fascinating feedback loop with neuroscience. The brain is an existence proof that intelligence is possible. We can take inspiration from it, build computational models, and then ask whether those models generate useful predictions about how the brain works. A system behaving like a human doesn’t necessarily mean it’s using the same mechanisms, but that comparison can still be very revealing.

And I think it helps us separate questions that we often bundle together. Solving a difficult problem, understanding the world, having a sense of self, having subjective experience—those may be related, but they aren’t obviously the same thing. If we build machines with increasingly general capabilities, we’ll have to get much clearer about those distinctions.

So, for me, the point isn’t simply to find a task that humans can do and machines can’t. That boundary will keep moving. It’s to understand the principles behind our minds, and perhaps, through that, understand what’s distinctive about the human experience.

r001.rationale: The response says building AI is one of the best ways to investigate what makes the human mind special and describes comparing AI models with the brain and human behavior.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that carbon-based and silicon-based substrates may process information differently.

r003.rationale: It mentions subjective experience but does not define consciousness as what processing information feels like.
